title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Cipher Suites for Transport Layer Security (TLS)
summary: Describes key exchange algorithms for TLS based on Elliptic Curve Cryptography, specifically ECDH key agreement in a handshake and ECDSA as an authentication mechanism. It is informational. It was replaced by RFC 8422.

eli5.summary: A newer, smaller kind of lock math for secure web connections. It keeps the secret strong while using less work. A later note replaced this one.

questions: what is the difference between ecdh and ecdhe
what does the supported elliptic curves extension do
subtitle: How TLS handshakes can use elliptic curve key agreement and signatures instead of larger RSA or DH keys.

tldr.problem: TLS handshakes of the time relied on RSA and classic Diffie-Hellman, which need large keys. That is costly for constrained and wireless devices.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds five ECC-based key exchange algorithms using ECDH key agreement, with ECDSA or RSA authentication. It also adds two ClientHello extensions to negotiate curves and point formats, and a set of new cipher suites.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC has been obsoleted by RFC 8422, and was also updated by RFC 5246, RFC 7027 and RFC 7919.

today: RFC 4492 is Informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 8422. It was also updated by RFC 5246, RFC 7027 and RFC 7919, so read the newer documents for current guidance.

sections.title: Why ECC for TLS
sections.content:
Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) offers security equivalent to RSA with smaller key sizes. The RFC gives a comparison table: a 163-bit ECC key is comparable to a 1024-bit DH/DSA/RSA key, and a 571-bit ECC key to a 15360-bit one. Smaller keys save power, memory, bandwidth and computation, which makes ECC attractive for constrained environments.

The document extends TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1. It defines the use of Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) key agreement, with long-term or ephemeral keys, to establish the TLS premaster secret. It also defines fixed-ECDH certificates and the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) for authenticating TLS peers.
sections.eli5: A small key can be as strong as a huge one if the math is cleverer. Smaller keys mean less work and less data to send.

sections.title: Five Key Exchange Algorithms
sections.content:
The RFC introduces five key exchange algorithms: ECDH_ECDSA, ECDHE_ECDSA, ECDH_RSA, ECDHE_RSA and ECDH_anon. All use ECDH to compute the TLS premaster secret. They differ only in the lifetime of the ECDH keys (long-term or ephemeral) and in how, if at all, those keys are authenticated. The derivation of the master secret and later keys is not changed.

  • ECDH_ECDSA: the server certificate holds an ECDH-capable key and is signed with ECDSA. No ServerKeyExchange is sent.
  • ECDHE_ECDSA: the server sends an ephemeral ECDH key and curve in ServerKeyExchange, signed with ECDSA.
  • ECDH_RSA and ECDHE_RSA: the same, except the certificate is signed with RSA (and for ECDHE_RSA the certificate holds an RSA signing key).
  • ECDH_anon: no certificates and no signatures, so it is open to man-in-the-middle attacks; implementations SHOULD authenticate by other means.

The ECDHE variants provide forward secrecy. The RFC notes that there is no structural difference between ECDH and ECDSA keys, and that X.509 key usage extensions can restrict what an ECC key may be used for.
sections.eli5: There are five recipes for agreeing on a secret. Some use a lock you keep for a long time, some use a fresh lock each time, and one skips checking who you are talking to at all.

sections.title: Client Authentication
sections.content:
Three client authentication mechanisms are named after the client certificate involved: ECDSA_sign, ECDSA_fixed_ECDH and RSA_fixed_ECDH. With ECDSA_sign the client proves it holds its private key by signing in a CertificateVerify message.

With the two fixed-ECDH mechanisms, the client certificate holds an ECDH key on the same curve as the server's long-term key, so the ClientKeyExchange message is empty and no CertificateVerify is sent. A successful exchange of Finished messages proves the client holds the matching private key. These two are usable with ECDH_ECDSA and ECDH_RSA, but their use with ECDHE_ECDSA and ECDHE_RSA is prohibited because a long-term client ECDH key would jeopardize forward secrecy.
sections.eli5: The visitor can show an ID card that works like a key, or sign a note to prove who they are. Either way the server can check they are real.

sections.title: Negotiating Curves and Point Formats
sections.content:
Two TLS extensions let a client say which curves and point formats it supports: elliptic_curves (extension type 10) and ec_point_formats (type 11). A client that proposes ECC cipher suites SHOULD include them, and a client that proposes none MUST NOT. The curve list is ordered by client preference. Named curves such as secp256r1 (value 23) are numbered 1 to 25, and the values 0xFF01 and 0xFF02 signal support for arbitrary explicit prime and characteristic-2 curves.

The point format list may include uncompressed (0), ansiX962_compressed_prime (1) and ansiX962_compressed_char2 (2). The uncompressed format MUST be supported and MUST appear in the list when the extension is sent. The server answers with its own point format list in ServerHello.

Servers MUST NOT negotiate an ECC cipher suite unless they can finish the handshake within the client's stated curves and formats, so an ECC handshake does not fail later. On session resumption the server ignores these extensions.
sections.eli5: Before talking, the client says which kinds of math it knows. The server only picks a kind the client understands, so nobody gets stuck halfway.

sections.title: Messages and Cipher Suites
sections.content:
ECC changes the content of several existing handshake messages: ClientHello, ServerHello, the server Certificate, ServerKeyExchange, CertificateRequest, the client Certificate, ClientKeyExchange and CertificateVerify.

In ServerKeyExchange, an ECCurveType says whether the curve is sent as explicit_prime (1), explicit_char2 (2) or named_curve (3); named curves SHOULD be used when applicable. For ECDHE_ECDSA, ECDHE_RSA and ECDH_anon the server sends its ephemeral public key as an ECPoint. A CertificateRequest can list ecdsa_sign (64), rsa_fixed_ecdh (65) and ecdsa_fixed_ecdh (66).

The shared ECDH secret is computed with ECKAS-DH1 from IEEE 1363, and the premaster secret is the x-coordinate of the shared point; leading zeros MUST NOT be truncated. ECDSA uses SHA-1 by default (sha_size is 20).

Section 6 defines new cipher suites with codes from { 0xC0, 0x01 } to { 0xC0, 0x19 }, in the forms such as TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA. Servers SHOULD support four listed suites and clients SHOULD support at least one of them: TLS_ECDH_ECDSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA, TLS_ECDH_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA and TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA.
sections.eli5: The messages in the handshake get a few new boxes to carry the curve and the public number. The note also gives each new combination of tools its own name tag.

sections.title: Security and Curve Choice
sections.content:
The security notes of TLS 1.0 and 1.1 apply to these handshakes. The RFC points to curve selection as the key ECC-specific issue: key size guidance is the comparison table in the introduction. Beyond size, it says it is more conservative to use curves with little algebraic structure, so random curves are more conservative than special curves such as Koblitz curves. Algebraic structure can still bring efficiency, so conservatism may need to be balanced against speed.

It also warns that widely used single curves risk catastrophic failure, since an attack on that curve could compromise many keys. On forward secrecy, only ECDHE_ECDSA or ECDHE_RSA, with ECDSA_sign for client authentication where needed, gives complete forward secrecy.
sections.eli5: Pick a strong enough lock, and be careful: if everyone uses the same kind of lock and it breaks, everyone is in trouble. Using a fresh lock each time keeps old secrets safe even if a key leaks later.
